title: Why value-based care hasn’t lowered your medical bills [PODCAST]
summary: Subscribe to The Podcast by KevinMD. Watch on YouTube. Catch up on old episodes! Everyone agrees health care should reward better outcomes at lower cost. So why hasn’t it happened? The answer is...
full_content:
Subscribe to The Podcast by KevinMD. Watch on YouTube. Catch up on old episodes!

Everyone agrees health care should reward better outcomes at lower cost. So why hasn’t it happened? The answer isn’t payment models or policy. It comes down to the everyday choices individual clinicians make, and whether anyone can actually see them. Jeanne Cohen, a health care analytics founder and CEO, argues that the value in value-based care lives in the quality of each clinical decision, not the contract structure around it. This episode is based on her article “The real reason value-based care has not delivered,” published on KevinMD. You will hear why roughly a quarter of U.S. health care spending traces back to unwarranted variation, how ordering an unnecessary scan exposes patients to harm and pushes organizations out of financial alignment, and why the data infrastructure to fix this finally exists. Cohen also explains where AI can help, where it can’t, and why it won’t lower costs on its own. If you want to understand what actually stands between the health care system and the outcomes it keeps promising, this conversation names it directly.

This episode is brought to you by ModMed.

Welcome to your new AI-Powered Practice from ModMed. We’re transforming specialty care by embedding AI Assistants across your entire workflow. Our all-in-one platform of EHR, patient engagement, practice management, and RCM helps reduce repetitive work while keeping you firmly in control.

Trained on de-identified data from nearly a billion patient encounters, this isn’t just smarter software. It’s a new way of working for specialty medicine, more efficient and more connected to the patient experience.

Start building your AI-Powered Practice at modmed.com.

VISIT SPONSOR → https://www.modmed.com/

SUBSCRIBE TO THE PODCAST → https://www.kevinmd.com/podcast

Transcript

Kevin Pho: Hi, and welcome to the show. Subscribe at KevinMD.com/podcast. Today, we welcome Jeanne Cohen. She’s a health care analytics founder and CEO. Today’s KevinMD article is “The real reason value-based care has not delivered.” Jeanne, welcome to the show.

Jeanne Cohen: Thank you. It’s lovely to be here.

Kevin Pho: All right. Let’s start by briefly sharing your story, and then tell us why you decided to write this article on KevinMD.

Jeanne Cohen: Thank you. Well, Motive Medical Intelligence really began with a mission that we’re still on, which was to identify evidence in health care and to make sure and certain that clinicians had access to it. We started some years ago looking at the increasing volume of evidence, too much for people to stay current with. Yet practitioners, clinicians, want to deliver the best care they can. And so we started looking at this from a decision support perspective, and we’re the first company to make clinical practice guidelines computable, able to be consumed by computers and delivered in the clinical workflow.

As we did more with that, we recognized we really needed better visibility into what clinicians were actually doing. That’s why we started Practicing Wisely, which looks at and evaluates the clinical decisions of individual clinicians. So we are looking at this across all clinical areas. We’re looking at individual decision-making according to the evidence, so we’re doing that comparison. It provides a unique visibility for clinicians into how they’re actually practicing, and this is very valuable from many, many perspectives.

I think none of us as human beings has a 360-degree view of ourselves, not personally or professionally. And really the gathering and presenting of this information is to return to our mission, which is to help people, help clinicians know what they need to know and act on what they need to know and what they do know.

Kevin Pho: All right. So you wrote the article “The real reason value-based care has not delivered.” Tell us why you decided to write this particular article, and then tell us about it for those who didn’t get a chance to read it.

Jeanne Cohen: Great. Well, because there is an absolute connection between individual clinician decisions, the quality of those decisions, and the achievement of the aims of value-based care, which is higher quality care at lower cost. It seemed that it was a good moment to talk about and make explicit this connection.

Value-based care has been something we’ve talked about for quite a while. I would say in the early years it was more of an incantation than a program, but I would say in the last five to seven years there’s been more value-based care, primarily in primary care, not specialists as much as primary care. But value-based care has been focused on payment, on payment mechanisms, and it’s been evaluating care at an organizational level or a process level. So nothing is looking at the key element of success in value-based care, which is the quality of the treatment, the quality of the clinical decisions. And this goes back many years to the seminal Wennberg article, I’m sure you know it, around variation in care as the source of costs and poor outcomes.

And so by looking at individual decisions, we are specifically looking at what we call appropriateness. Was the care necessary? Addressing the unwarranted variation in care. In a fee-for-service system, variation can be buried within volume. In a value-based care system, variation is exposure. It’s structural exposure, it’s care quality exposure, it’s cost exposure. So it seemed, because there is now, I think, another wave of movement toward value-based care for many reasons, like an important moment to start talking about this next level of value-based care, which requires a new way of looking at performance measurement, sort of performance measurement 2.0.

Kevin Pho: And what are some of the reasons why value-based care hasn’t really achieved the aims that you describe?

Jeanne Cohen: Well, there are multiple. It’s like everything in health care. It’s multifactorial. So a lot of the focus initially had to be on the data infrastructure. In order to do value-based care, you had to have data. You had to know what your results were. You had to gather that information. I think health care, when we started talking about value-based care, really underestimated the infrastructure deficiencies, which meant that data was not flowing, the data that was needed, so it took years for that to happen.

You also have the regulatory environment and misaligned incentives. So in the beginning it was carrots, or carrots and sticks, but neither were significant enough to really motivate that change. And I also think organizations struggle with the investment that needs to be made in the change to workflows and the change to operations to bring value-based care in.

I think while we all attached ourselves enthusiastically to the goal of value-based care, which is not only laudable, it’s imperative, I think as an industry we underestimated the steps that needed to be taken to get there. And so we have ended with years of talking about it and working at it, but it has not been as broadly adopted as people would hope. But I think we’re in a place now where that absolutely can happen. I think people want it to happen.

Kevin Pho: So you’re saying that now we do have that technology, we do have that data infrastructure where we can realize some of the goals of value-based care? Do we still have room to move, or do you think that where we are now, we should be able to realize those goals?

Jeanne Cohen: I think we should be able to realize those goals. I think the infrastructure is there, I think the mechanisms are there. And again, so much of the early emphasis was really on the payment structures, on the how of it, not on where the value is in value-based care. We have to get back to the fact that the value is in the quality of care. The value is in the interaction there between the patient and the clinician, and that’s the part that we’re focusing on.

We’re helping to define that value and actually quantify that value, which now makes it possible to go forward in value-based arrangements, because without this visibility into clinician decision-making, you are at risk in a value-based care arrangement. If you do not know the particulars of that, you are at risk on the cost and quality side.

Kevin Pho: So you wrote in your article that the success of value-based care, like you said, hinges on individual clinical decisions rather than policy or payer contracts. So give us an example or scenario of how that individual clinical decision can really impact the goals of value-based care.

Jeanne Cohen: Well, value-based care arrangements are all payments in which there are reimbursement rates tied to how the care is delivered and the volume of care and all of those things, and if you have a clinician who is, for whatever reason, overutilizing, for example, expensive nuclear imaging, you will simply be out of alignment with all of the commitments on the financial side, and you will also be exposing patients unnecessarily, for example, to radiation.

So when we talk about appropriateness of care, we’re sort of looking at three vectors: care that’s high cost, care that has the potential for harm to the patient, and care that’s practiced with unwarranted variation in terms of the evidence. So this is a very fundamental element in value-based care, that you need to be practicing appropriately, not overusing, but also not underusing. We’re also looking at underuse, which is close to preventive care, and we can analyze, in terms of those decisions, the downstream health impact to the patient and the cost to the system of not doing those things. So you really see the clinician decision as the fulcrum of value in this value-based care structure.

Kevin Pho: In your article, you wrote that about 25 percent of U.S. health care spending is wasteful or linked to variation. How much of that is actually recoverable, I guess, under an ideal scenario of how value-based care should be executed?

Jeanne Cohen: Well, we would argue that most of it is recoverable, and it depends on how an organization wants to use it. We can see that this kind of visibility is being used by provider and payer organizations in a number of ways. For example, to put information about clinical decisions in front of primary care physicians so they can refer to specialists who are practicing at a high level, with a high-value, high-appropriateness score. They are also using it, obviously, to steer patients to higher-value providers. They’re using it to form and shape networks, and using it for prior authorization.

So all of these are ways of deploying this, and also using it to educate physicians, to say, “Here’s what we see you’re doing. Here’s how you compare to your peers for this particular intervention, for this kind of patient. Let’s talk about that.” So it’s a way of informing physicians. When we talk to physicians and work with them on the results of their measurement, they’re very open. This is information they haven’t had before.

And you’ll find that this is not related to malfeasance. It’s related to all kinds of much less dramatic and certainly not pernicious things. For example, in one organization there was tremendous overuse of nuclear imaging prior to some kind of therapy, and it turned out that they didn’t have an echocardiogram program in place, which would have enabled them to do that. So many of these things that prevent people from operating on what they know, doing what they know is the best thing, are operational. So this is also valuable to organizations to help them redesign their workflows and make other kinds of modalities available.

Kevin Pho: What’s the current landscape just in general? Because I know that there are some organizations who are doing exactly what we’re discussing today in terms of being transparent and adjusting the workflows and giving that information to clinicians to influence their practices, and of course, some organizations that are not that far down the line. So in general, what’s the current landscape of physician practices when it comes to that transparency of data in order to realize the value of value-based care?

Jeanne Cohen: I think there is much more welcoming of it. I think there’s much more adoption and welcoming. I think physicians, clinicians, now know that measurement can be a positive. This is not about being punitive. This is about informing. So I would say I’m very encouraged. I would say there is near-universal agreement that information like this can be valuable. I think there is a recommitment to making the kinds of changes and investments that need to be made to make this possible, and it’s also become an imperative from a financial and cost perspective. So I think the landscape is good.

Kevin Pho: So do you think that in order to realize the full potential of value-based care, there does need to be more of a policy shift? Because there is still a substantial portion of our health care system that is still fee-for-service, and isn’t that just going to be a permanent impediment to the full realization of value-based care?

Jeanne Cohen: I think possibly. I think there are two things. I think CMS has certainly stated that its objective is to have everyone in Medicare Advantage, which is a form of a value-based care program, obviously a capitated program, by a certain time. I think regulatory policy can help, but the record in health care is not that it always helps. I think some support may be necessary, but it can’t be heavy-handed. I think the government is aware that becoming too involved in the daily operation of medicine in various organizations is probably not a good thing. I think there are things maybe from a reimbursement perspective that could be done that would incentivize people to move more quickly.

Kevin Pho: Now, if you were in charge of our health care system or in charge of Medicare and you were to set policy, tell us what you would like to see in an ideal scenario.

Jeanne Cohen: I think probably it would be much more public discussion about the relationship between the daily activities of health care and the achievement of these goals. Sometimes this is separate. The policy discussion is at another level, as if it has no relationship to what people are doing every single day. I think that would be something that would galvanize the industry to do more, and it would also educate in a way that I think is not clear now. It is surprising when you talk to organizations and to clinicians, the lack of awareness of the connection between the decisions they’re making on a daily basis and performance under value-based care.

Kevin Pho: So are you talking about maybe publicizing some of the quality data? Because I know that we all have quality data. I’m a physician, I get this presented to me. But making those more public, like you said, would galvanize behavior?

Jeanne Cohen: I think so, and you’re seeing some of that already. I think that in terms of the steerage, the various activities around member steerage, those sites and those solutions are showing more and more information to consumers. I think one of the things that’s always been talked about in health care is that consumer power, informed consumers, will help to push change in health care. I do think we’re seeing more of that.

When someone wants to select a physician, they no longer feel as comfortable necessarily just taking what’s offered or what the plan says. They do want more information, and certainly we are supporting solutions, many solutions like that, with information. So I think, again, a much more open sharing of the data and the information, and the reason why that information is important, would galvanize the community beyond what I think is already an increasing and solid set of commitments to try to get there.

Kevin Pho: Now we’re talking, of course, about health care data, so I need to ask about the impact of artificial intelligence. Where do you see the impact of AI affecting the transparency of data, the analysis of data, or even the collection of data going forward?

Jeanne Cohen: Well, of course, it’s huge. I think AI is an analytical tool and can be applied that way. It’s clear to everyone that there are immediate things that can be done to improve productivity that AI can help with. I think in the areas we’re talking about, which is evaluating clinical decisions and so on, I think there you’re going to have a hybrid. Medicine, the practice of medicine, will always need a hybrid approach. AI is a tool that can support, but it can’t replace the human in the loop. And I think while there’s tremendous early enthusiasm for all of this, naturally, we’re going to end at a place where there’s a much more thoughtful and nuanced approach that combines them both.

I think one of the implications of AI, however, is that the skill sets that are going to be valued in health care, as well as everywhere else, are going to shift, and judgment, the ability to discern, discernment and trust, are going to become two very critical parts of what individuals, including clinicians, bring to the world they’re practicing in.

But I think also, and I agree with David Brailer here, I do not think AI is going to impact affordability in health care. I think it will scale and accelerate the pace at which the incentives are deployed, the payment incentives are deployed. I think it’s still the payment system itself that’s going to determine affordability, and that’s something that we all know needs to be looked at, worked on, and changed.

Kevin Pho: We’re talking to Jeanne Cohen. She’s a health care analytics founder and CEO. Today’s KevinMD article is “The real reason value-based care has not delivered.” Jeanne, let’s end with your take-home messages that you want to leave with the KevinMD audience.

Jeanne Cohen: I think the future of health care is bright. I think health care has two things. It has authentic complexity, because it truly is unlike any other industry. It’s existential, it’s human, it’s authentically complex. There also is in health care a great deal of false complication, and so we need always to sort those two things. Where is the authentic complexity, and where can we support and help there and eliminate false complication? So, you know, health care is hard, but the future is bright. It’s hard for the right reasons, and it’s a privilege to be part of health care.

Kevin Pho: Jeanne, thank you so much for sharing your perspective and insight, and thanks again for coming on the show.

Jeanne Cohen: Thank you so much for inviting me.

title: Breast implant removal leaves patients paying 3 times
summary: Former cosmetic surgeon Robert Yoho, MD, after retiring from medical practice in 2019, became an author and health care whistleblower and recently addressed the “explant” trend in which br...
full_content:
Former cosmetic surgeon Robert Yoho, MD, after retiring from medical practice in 2019, became an author and health care whistleblower and recently addressed the “explant” trend in which breast implants are surgically removed. According to the American Society of Plastic Surgeons, 306,196 women bought breast augmentation in 2024. In 2021, the FDA added a boxed warning to implants cautioning that they are linked to breast implant-associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma (BIA-ALCL), squamous cell carcinoma, and systemic symptoms known as breast implant illness (BII). Complications increase over time, adds the warning. As people reconsider or decline implants, are there market implications?

“The backlash does not threaten that model. It extends it,” says Dr. Yoho. “Explant, dissolving, restoration, and revision are all billable, all cash, and all performed on women who have already proved they will pay. Insurance usually refuses to pay for the removal on the grounds that the first operation was cosmetic. So, the woman who paid to put them in pays again to take them out, at a higher price, and pays a third time to rebuild what is left.”

According to Dr. Yoho, silicone gel implants rupture silently (which is why the FDA suggests getting baseline scans), but when a saline implant fails, the recipient knows within a day, because the breast goes flat. Yet warnings are scarce in a system that he says is a closed loop.

“The [cosmetic surgery] consultation is a sales meeting run by a man in a white coat and the product is an operation on a healthy body,” he cautions. “Almost nowhere else in medicine are the diagnosing doctor, the treating doctor, and the salesman the same person, with nobody else in the room.”

Dr. Yoho adds that studies given to prospective patients are “designed, paid for, and published by the people selling the device” and that a woman who started surgeries at 25 has “spent the price of a house down payment on a body” by buying a device that will need replacing for the next foreseeable 60 years. To protect themselves, patients should ask the surgeon how many procedures he did last year and how many revisions he performed on his own patients. They should also ask a surgeon what his repeat-surgery rate is at 10 years, whether the changes are permanent and, if not, what the upkeep costs will be.

People who pursue cosmetic surgery, especially repeat patients, may suffer from mental issues according to medical literature, and it’s a real problem, says Dr. Yoho. Body dysmorphic disorder, in which the person is tormented by a flaw other people cannot see, drives about one patient in seven, he calculates, and is often worsened by surgery.

“Nobody in any of these rooms checks the patient’s mind. Here is a psychiatric condition present in 15 percent of the customers, which the product reliably worsens, and which nobody in the industry has a financial reason to find. If Pharma sold a drug with that profile, the class-action lawyers would own the company. In cosmetics it is called a busy practice.”

Martha Rosenberg is an investigative reporter whose work has appeared in the British Medical Journal (BMJ), Consumer Reports, Public Citizen, the Center for Health Journalism at USC Annenberg, the Nieman Foundation for Journalism at Harvard University, and other outlets. She studied at Rush Medical School and writes on health care, food, medicine, and public policy.

Rosenberg’s reporting has been cited by Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, Mayo Clinic Proceedings, Public Library of Science Biology, ScienceDirect, the Journal of Pain & Palliative Care Pharmacotherapy, the Journal of Trauma & Dissociation, Britannica, National Geographic, Hastings Law Journal, and Wikipedia. She is the author of several books, including Multidisciplinary Management of Chronic Pain: A Practical Guide for Clinicians, Born With a Junk Food Deficiency, Big Food, Big Pharma, Big Lies, and Food, Clothes, Men, Gas and Other Problems. She publishes on Substack, OpEdNews, and her Amazon author page.

title: Medical gaslighting delayed my diagnosis by 20 years
summary: This is dedicated to my fellow Zebras. I hear you. I see you. This is not an easy story to share, but I want to do so in the hope of bringing greater visibility to conditions that are often overlooked...
full_content:
This is dedicated to my fellow Zebras. I hear you. I see you.

This is not an easy story to share, but I want to do so in the hope of bringing greater visibility to conditions that are often overlooked and poorly understood. This reflection explores my experience as both a patient and doctor navigating hypermobility and its associated conditions. My aim is to help reduce delays in diagnosis, encourage clinicians to listen to and believe patients’ experiences, highlight the consequences of fragmented care and diagnostic uncertainty, encourage greater clinical advocacy, and promote more compassionate, informed, and coordinated care for patients who too often feel that they do not belong anywhere within the health care system.

Writing this makes me vulnerable. As a rheumatology advanced trainee, I know that expressing these views may invite judgment from colleagues and senior doctors, particularly when I am challenging attitudes within my own profession. But I also feel a responsibility to use the voice I have. I have spent many years experiencing what it is like to be the patient who does not have an explanation, who does not know where to turn, and who has to advocate for themselves simply to be heard. Many patients do not have the medical knowledge or professional position that I have had. If I remain silent despite having experienced this from both sides, I cannot expect those patients to be heard either.

If sharing my experience can help another patient feel believed, help a clinician recognize a condition they might otherwise overlook, or encourage our profession to reconsider how we approach these patients, then I believe it is worth making myself vulnerable in doing so. Why now? Because I finally have the answers I spent years searching for. Because I have carried this experience largely alone, and it is finally time for me to talk.

In 2022, I was diagnosed with hypermobility spectrum disorder (HSD) and postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS). It took almost twenty years to receive these diagnoses, during which I experienced prolonged diagnostic uncertainty, dismissal of symptoms, and multiple occasions of medical gaslighting. This journey was marked by frustration, grief, suffering, and the challenges of living with conditions that were invisible to others.

Shortly after receiving these diagnoses, I disclosed them to a doctor friend. Their response was, “Aren’t those conditions all in your head?” I remember feeling shocked and speechless. After finally obtaining answers following years of symptoms and uncertainty, I had not expected my experiences to be immediately questioned. That moment highlighted for me the significant lack of awareness and persistent misconceptions that continue to surround many invisible illnesses, even within the medical profession itself.

Several years later, as a rheumatology registrar, I have become increasingly aware of the attitudes that can surround hypermobility and its associated conditions within medicine. I have heard comments questioning the legitimacy of patients’ symptoms, frustration about the clinical time and resources these patients require, and suggestions that hypermobility does not have a place within rheumatology. I have also heard colleagues describe lengthy consultations with hypermobile patients as time that could have been better spent elsewhere.

These conversations have taken on a different meaning since disclosing my own diagnoses to colleagues within the rheumatology profession, that I trusted. On occasions, I have found myself present while the very conditions I live with were discussed dismissively or treated as a source of humor, right in front of me, by the very colleagues who knew my diagnosis. I did not always know how to respond. Instead, I often sat quietly, aware of the uncomfortable gap between what was being said and what my colleagues knew about my own experience. HSD and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS) are not a joke or a funny matter. It has led to young patients seeking voluntary assisted dying for their conditions.

Invisible illnesses

Invisible illnesses are not uncommon. In Australia, 1 in 6 people lives with a disability, and approximately 80 percent of these disabilities are invisible in nature. Despite their prevalence, 1 in 10 Australians living with disability has experienced discrimination in the past year. Furthermore, as life expectancy increases and people live longer with chronic diseases, the number of years lived with disability due to chronic conditions has risen substantially, from 1.6 million in 2003 to 2.5 million in 2023.

There is a historical context to how we understand some of these illnesses. For centuries, unexplained physical symptoms in women were often attributed to “female hysteria.” Although this diagnosis has long since disappeared from modern medicine, its history is an important reminder of how easily physical symptoms that are poorly understood can be attributed to psychological causes, particularly when they occur predominantly in women. This includes female-predominant conditions such as HSD, EDS, polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, fibromyalgia, endometriosis, and chronic pelvic pain disorders. Medicine has undoubtedly progressed, but the experiences of patients today remind us that the underlying challenge has not entirely disappeared. The language may have changed, but the risk of dismissing symptoms because they are difficult to explain remains.

This is particularly relevant as patients are increasingly becoming well informed about their symptoms and potential diagnoses and seeking answers from specialists after years of uncertainty. Patients are often arriving at consultations having spent years researching their symptoms, joining support groups, and attempting to understand what their bodies are experiencing. For many, it reflects the reality that they have had to become experts in their own symptoms because no one else has yet been able to provide them with an explanation.

As awareness grows, the number of individuals seeking assessment and care for these conditions will continue to rise. The health care system must recognize this changing landscape and create the capacity, expertise, and pathways necessary to provide timely, compassionate, and evidence-based care for this growing patient population.

Being my own multidisciplinary coordinator

For many patients with HSD or EDS (which encompasses thirteen subtypes), the experience extends far beyond joint hypermobility. Associated conditions and complications can include mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS), small fiber neuropathy, pelvic organ prolapse, abdominopelvic compression syndromes, and neurodivergence. As a result, many of us find ourselves navigating an increasingly complex network of specialists.

When I was first diagnosed, I saw a cardiologist, clinical geneticist, ophthalmologist, immunologist, pain specialist, general physician, neurologist, and clinical pharmacologist, in addition to several allied health professionals. For my multiple symptoms, I trialed a vagus nerve stimulation device, low-dose naltrexone, and a variety of other medications.

It was a lonely and isolating experience. I am the only person in my family with the condition, trying to understand a diagnosis that was new to me while navigating its many manifestations. Despite being a doctor, I often felt that I had little ability to advocate effectively for myself.

In many ways, I became the coordinator of my own multidisciplinary care. I collected letters from one specialist to take to the next, repeatedly retold my history, and tried to piece together a coherent understanding of what was happening to me. There was little communication between the clinicians involved in my care, and the responsibility for connecting the dots often fell to me. When I was not believed, I collected medical literature to show to my GPs so I could get the referrals I needed. It was a horrendous experience.

The irony was that the very process of coordinating my care became another source of cognitive burden. The stress of navigating multiple appointments and advocating for myself often exacerbated brain fog. There were times when I would attend a specialist appointment already anxious about having to explain and justify my symptoms, only to leave afterwards struggling to remember what we had discussed due to brain fog.

Even as a doctor, with the medical knowledge and health literacy that should have made navigating the system easier, I found myself overwhelmed by the complexity of trying to coordinate my own care. I often wonder how much more difficult this must be for patients without a medical background.

Perhaps this is one of the greatest difficulties for patients with complex and multisystem conditions: We are often not just patients receiving care. We become the people responsible for coordinating it.

Growing up without an explanation

The diagnosis that proved most difficult for me to obtain was an explanation for my severe, medication-refractory constipation. My symptoms began when I was around eleven or twelve years old. Alongside symptoms that I now recognize as dysautonomia, I developed increasingly severe constipation and abdominal bloating. As a child, there were times when I would spend hours sitting on the toilet in severe pain, screaming as I tried to open my bowels. By my early teenage years, the bloating was so significant that I often looked pregnant, and was asked by strangers “how far along” I was.

I saw a gastroenterologist, who felt that I had irritable bowel syndrome. However, the severity of my symptoms continued to escalate. I was admitted to hospital with fecal loading and required bowel preparation to clear my bowels. Yet, despite the severity of my symptoms, there was still no clear explanation.

I was subsequently referred to a gastrointestinal motility specialist, but again, no definitive answer was found. I was barely investigated. I progressed through increasingly intensive treatments for constipation, including prucalopride, with little benefit.

At the same time, other symptoms were occurring that, in retrospect, were also part of a much larger picture. As a teenager, I saw a cardiologist because of chest pain. It was attributed to anxiety. I did not question this explanation at the time. When you are young, and a doctor tells you that your symptoms are anxiety, you assume they must be right.

Medical school did not give me answers

I entered medical school without a diagnosis. By the time I was studying medicine, my gastrointestinal symptoms had become severe enough that I was reduced to manually disimpacting myself because my rectum simply would not evacuate normally.

I was learning about hundreds of diseases, memorizing their presentations and understanding increasingly complex physiology, yet I never once learned about EDS, HSD, POTS, or many of the conditions that would eventually explain my own experience. The irony is difficult to ignore. I was training to diagnose other people while lacking the knowledge to understand what was happening to my own body.

I remember sitting in a car with a heart rate of 140 beats per minute. I had been told previously that my symptoms were anxiety, but I did not feel anxious. I continued to have episodes where my heart would race, accompanied by chest discomfort and a sense that something was seriously wrong. I would call my family and tell them that I thought I was having a heart attack. But I did not seek medical attention, because I had already learned that they would probably be attributed to anxiety.

Basic Physician Training while living with an undiagnosed illness

I studied for my Basic Physician Training examinations while experiencing symptoms of undiagnosed POTS. Again, these conditions were not part of the formal education I received during Basic Training. I had no framework through which to understand the relationship between my tachycardia, exercise intolerance, gastrointestinal dysfunction, brain fog, and other symptoms. There is a particular kind of helplessness in having symptoms that affect your daily life while still being unable to explain them, not because you have not looked, but because you do not yet know what you are looking for.

I sat my Basic Training examinations and passed them on my first attempt, despite studying through a significant flare of symptoms. I had always been determined. Perhaps that determination is part of why it took me so long to recognize how unwell I was. I kept going. I adapted. I took the elevator instead of the stairs to see the patient on level 5, and I learned how to manage my bowels myself. I found ways to function because I did not know that there might be another explanation.

Advanced Training, the increasing isolation and loneliness

After relocating interstate to pursue Advanced Training, I requested copies of my previous gastroenterology records so that I could provide them to my new gastroenterologist. I had never personally reviewed these documents before. Reading them brought me to my knees in tears. To my shock, my longstanding need for manual disimpaction had been attributed to obsessive compulsive disorder.

As a young woman, I had been forced to perform this distressing and deeply embarrassing act, often multiple times a day, removing pellet-like stool from my rectum because I lacked the normal urge to defecate. To see these symptoms reduced to a psychiatric explanation was devastating.

Looking back, it became apparent that alternative diagnoses had not been fully explored. I had never even undergone a colonoscopy, which now seems extraordinary given the severity and duration of my symptoms. At the time, I was a medical student and did not know enough to question whether further investigations should have been pursued.

It was only last year, twelve years since starting to manually disimpact, that I was referred to a colorectal surgeon who undertook the comprehensive evaluation I had always needed. This included a colonoscopy with rectal biopsies and investigations such as gastric emptying studies, small bowel studies, and ultimately a defecating proctogram. I will never forget the memory of when I finally received a diagnosis for the reasons why my rectum did not work properly.

The defecating proctogram that ultimately provided these answers is only available at certain centers in Australia and at limited times throughout the year. I undertook it while doing rheumatology Advanced Training. I traveled interstate alone, by bus, to undergo the test. Before the procedure, the radiologist asked about my symptoms. I remember saying, “I’ve been told it’s all in my head. All the previous investigations have been inconclusive. I don’t know why I bothered coming here today because this test will probably be inconclusive too.” I then briefly described years of manual disimpaction, severe constipation, bloating, and the profound impact these symptoms had on my quality of life.

He listened quietly and proceeded with the test. After I had expelled as much of the barium paste as I could, he asked if I was certain I was finished. I said yes. He encouraged me to try again, and to my surprise, more came out. He then paused the images and pointed to the screen. “This,” he said, “is a rectal intussusception.”

I had heard of intussusception occurring elsewhere in the bowel, but never in the rectum. I was stunned. He continued, “It’s not in your head. This is one of the common causes of chronic constipation in women and is related to pelvic floor dysfunction.”

Someone had finally validated what I had been going through. I finally had an answer. For several seconds, the world seemed to stand still. I remember wanting to hug him while sitting on a commode.

I cried tears of relief that answers had finally arrived. I cried for the years spent suffering without an explanation, for the countless episodes of dismissal and medical gaslighting, for grieving the loss of a normal bodily function at a young age, and for the uncertainty of what this diagnosis meant for my future, including the possibility of surgery. Most of all, I cried over the question that so many people with chronic illness ask themselves: “Why me?”

The final report later revealed not only a high-grade rectal intussusception, but also a rectocele and rectal prolapse. The underlying abnormalities in my connective tissue had affected my pelvic floor, my gastrointestinal function, and many other aspects of my body. The simple act of opening one’s bowels normally, something most people take for granted, became something I longed for.

Much of my journey with chronic illness was experienced alone, including investigations and procedures. Training required me to relocate frequently, often leaving me without established support networks. This is another aspect of navigating medical conditions among doctors that deserves greater recognition: Who are our support networks when we have to pack up and leave again and again for training?

Despite these challenges, I have been fortunate. I do not consider myself disabled by my condition, and I have been able to continue working full time without workplace adjustments, unlike many others living with hypermobility and associated disorders.

Being too scared to share

On medical officer job advertisements, there is often a statement about inclusion and diversity, reflecting an understandable commitment to creating workplaces in which people from different backgrounds and with different experiences feel welcomed and supported. Yet, throughout my training, I have not always felt that these principles were meaningfully reflected in practice.

Inclusion is not simply about whether someone is offered a position or whether an organization can demonstrate diversity on paper. It is also about whether people feel safe to disclose their circumstances, whether their differences are understood rather than judged, whether appropriate support is available when difficulties arise, and whether they are treated with the same dignity and respect as their colleagues.

For someone living with an invisible condition, this distinction becomes particularly important. A person may appear well, perform at a high level and meet all of the expectations of their role, while simultaneously navigating symptoms and challenges that are not visible to those around them. Disclosure should not result in a person subsequently feeling scrutinized, perceived differently, or made to feel that their health is an inconvenience.

I have come to understand that inclusion is tested not when everything is going well, but when someone becomes vulnerable. It is easy for an organization to state that it values diversity. The more meaningful question is what happens when an employee or trainee discloses something personal, asks for support, or does not fit neatly into the expected mold of a doctor or trainee.

I have not been fortunate enough to consistently experience that distinction between the values expressed in recruitment material and the reality of being a trainee. This has made me reflect on how much more needs to be done to ensure that inclusion and diversity are not simply statements accompanying a job advertisement, but principles that are genuinely experienced by the people working within the organization.

The irony is that medicine frequently speaks about inclusion and diversity, yet invisible disability can expose how conditional that inclusion sometimes is. We often celebrate diversity when it is visible and easily understood; we struggle more when someone’s difference is invisible, fluctuating, or difficult to explain.

For much of my career, I chose not to disclose my condition. Early on, I became aware of the stigma that can surround being a doctor with a chronic condition and worried that disclosure could affect future career opportunities. I had a friend who had a chronic condition, well managed, who was told to leave the workplace when she disclosed. I sought advice from colleagues who told me never to disclose my condition.

I remember interviewing for a competitive rheumatology Advanced Training position. I carefully considered whether to disclose my hypermobility diagnosis and lived experience of chronic illness. I hoped that it would be viewed positively, as a source of empathy, insight, and motivation to care for patients living with similar conditions.

In the interview, I chose to speak openly about my diagnosis, framing it as a strength rather than a limitation. I discussed my desire to contribute to the care of patients with hypermobility disorders, recognizing that rheumatologists are often involved in diagnosing and managing these conditions. I emphasized that my condition had never affected my ability to work or fulfill my professional responsibilities and explained how my experiences had deepened my understanding of the challenges faced by individuals living with chronic and often invisible illnesses. I believed that these experiences would allow me to provide more compassionate, patient-centered care and advocate for patients who frequently feel unheard or misunderstood.

I was unsuccessful in obtaining the position. When I later sought feedback from the head interviewer, I was advised, “It would be wise not to discuss any medical conditions you have.”

I remember feeling stupid, ashamed, embarrassed, and deeply disheartened. I struggled to comprehend that a doctor, or perhaps even an interview panel of doctors, might perceive an invisible medical condition as a liability rather than recognizing the strengths and perspectives it could bring.

I interviewed the following year, not disclosing my condition, and got onto the program. I became very good at not speaking about my conditions, and pretending that I was like everyone else, because my conditions were invisible.

Since entering rheumatology training, and experiencing what it is like to have these conditions questioned or dismissed within the medical profession, I have slowly found my voice. I remember being present for a rheumatology consultation involving a patient with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. I had previously disclosed my own diagnosis to the rheumatologist. As we reviewed the patient’s history and numerous medical conditions, the rheumatologist asked, “How could this patient be a psychologist?” I remember feeling ashamed of having the very conditions I had disclosed. The same question could have been asked of me: How could I be a doctor?

On another occasion, I attended a gastroenterology-rheumatology multidisciplinary meeting involving consultants and registrars from both specialties. We were discussing several complex patients when a gastroenterologist described a patient with fibromyalgia and hypermobility and asked whether these conditions were “in the patient’s head,” stating that she felt they were.

I was shocked. What surprised me almost as much was that no one else in the room challenged the comment. I gathered the courage to stand up at the back of the room and say, “No, these conditions are not in the patient’s head. There can certainly be psychological consequences associated with living with these conditions, but there is substantial research supporting an underlying biological basis.”

The meeting continued as though I had said nothing. No one spoke up in support of what I had said. I felt deeply disappointed that, despite being in a room full of rheumatologists, I was standing alone.

I recognized something had changed in me. I could no longer remain silent. I had spent years learning how to hide my conditions so that I could be perceived as “like everyone else.” Now, I was beginning to understand that speaking openly could be part of changing how patients like me are perceived within medicine.

The importance of medical education

About two years ago, I responded to a Royal Australasian College of Physicians (RACP) request for suggestions of medical conditions that should be included in the College Learning Series (CLS). I replied saying that there should be greater education about HSD and EDS and its associated conditions. I was advised by the college that EDS was considered “relatively rare and specialized,” and that there were many conditions the college would like to include but could not accommodate within the size of the program.

I understand that medical curricula cannot cover every condition. However, I found the characterization of EDS as simply rare difficult to reconcile, with the combined prevalence of HSD and hypermobile EDS (hEDS), the most common subtype, estimated at approximately 1 in 600 to 900 people. POTS affects approximately 0.2 percent of the population. By comparison, Marfan syndrome has an estimated prevalence of approximately 1 in 5,000, yet receives considerably greater representation in Basic Physician Training curricula. I relayed these statistics to the college. The response was, “At this stage, CLS isn’t willing to include EDS/POTS as a topic.”

This is not an argument that these conditions should replace other diseases in the curriculum. It is an argument for recognition. For patients who may spend years searching for an explanation, even basic clinician awareness can make an enormous difference.

The hard truth of being a rheumatology trainee with hypermobility

Hypermobility has an important role within rheumatology. Rheumatologists are specialists in the assessment of joints, musculoskeletal disease, and connective tissue disorders, and are therefore well placed to assess patients presenting with significant hypermobility and determine whether further specialist investigation is required.

My concern is not that every patient with hypermobility needs ongoing rheumatology follow-up. Nor do I underestimate the pressures facing rheumatology services. Waiting lists are long, referral volumes are high, and there is a well-recognized shortage of rheumatologists across Australia. The Australian Rheumatology Association has highlighted that Australia has approximately 506 practicing adult rheumatologists, compared with a projected requirement of 749 to meet population need.

As a rheumatology trainee, I found myself in the uncomfortable position of being responsible for rejecting referrals for patients referred with hypermobility. This was particularly difficult when I understood the potential importance of an initial rheumatological assessment.

Any appropriately trained doctor may be able to diagnose HSD/EDS, but that does not mean rheumatology has nothing to contribute. A rheumatologist is well placed to assess whether a presentation is consistent with HSD or another connective tissue disorder, consider important alternative diagnoses, identify features that may warrant clinical genetics assessment, including where a vascular EDS phenotype is suspected, and facilitate appropriate baseline assessment and onward management where indicated.

I am not suggesting that every patient with hypermobility requires rheumatology assessment or ongoing rheumatology care. Nor am I suggesting that rheumatologists should carry the sole responsibility of caring for these patients. Our needs are often complex and individual, with some patients requiring more intensive input from other specialties. Rather, I believe there needs to be a clear pathway through which patients with significant symptoms or diagnostic uncertainty can access clinicians with appropriate expertise, including rheumatologists where appropriate. Once an appropriate diagnosis has been established and serious alternative diagnoses considered, ongoing care can be appropriately shared with primary care, allied health, and other relevant specialties. Rheumatologists are well placed to refer to many of the subspecialties and allied health services required by these patients.

A long waiting list reflects a systems problem, including workforce availability, funding and resource allocation, triage processes, and geographic distribution of specialists. I do not have all the answers to these system-level challenges, but collectively we need to start thinking about solutions. There are many rheumatologists actively taking on these patients and recognizing their importance in the patient’s health care journey. Part of the solution may ultimately involve clearer referral pathways, defined criteria for rheumatological assessment, further education for general practitioners and other specialists, multidisciplinary models of care, and appropriate discharge back to community-based management once serious pathology and relevant connective tissue disorders have been considered.

We also need greater investment in research into these conditions, which have for too long received limited attention in medical research and clinical education. Each specialty involved in a patient’s care should also communicate with one another, rather than leaving the patient to become the coordinator of their own health care.

Looking forward

I have spent much of my life trying to understand what was happening to my body. I have also spent much of my career learning how to understand what is happening to other people’s bodies. Living on both sides of the consultation has changed the way I practice medicine.

I know that medicine cannot always provide an immediate answer. I know that health care systems are under pressure, that specialists are overstretched, and that not every patient can be seen by every specialist. But I also know what it feels like to sit on the other side of the consultation room, anxious and exhausted, after years of searching for an explanation. Sometimes what a patient needs most is not an immediate diagnosis or a perfect treatment plan, but to know that someone believes them, is willing to listen, and will help them find the next step.

I look forward to the day when we have multidisciplinary, streamlined clinics specializing in the assessment and management of EDS, HSD, POTS, and their associated conditions. Clinics where rheumatologists, gastroenterologists, clinical geneticists, immunologists, neurologists, and psychiatrists work alongside allied health professionals, including exercise physiologists, physiotherapists, dietitians, social workers, and occupational therapists, to provide genuinely coordinated care. I look forward to the day when a patient living in rural or regional Australia can access this expertise through telehealth, without having to repeatedly travel hundreds of kilometers to see individual specialists. I look forward to the day when a patient living nearby can see multiple members of the multidisciplinary team within one or two coordinated visits, rather than navigating a fragmented system over years. I look forward to the day when these clinicians sit around the same table and discuss each patient’s presentation together, integrating their different perspectives to develop a coordinated and individualized pathway of care. I look forward to the day when we have expanded research into these conditions so we better understand them to better treat them. Most of all, I look forward to the day when we no longer have patients waiting twenty years to receive a diagnosis, to finally have their experiences recognized, their symptoms understood, and their care appropriately coordinated.

I have finally found answers to many of the questions I spent years asking. I now feel able to speak about the experiences that I once carried quietly. I hope that by doing so, I can contribute, in however small a way, to a health care system in which patients with invisible and poorly understood conditions no longer have to become their own advocates, coordinators, and experts simply to be heard.

Resources

Mogeshni Govender is a rheumatology advanced trainee with the Royal Australasian College of Physicians (RACP), with a background in hematology and internal medicine. Govender holds a Bachelor of Medical Sciences and a Doctor of Medicine.

Clinical and research interests center on hypermobility and its associated conditions, and on the connective tissue diseases. Alongside training, Govender writes about medicine, advocates for patients, and works toward a better health care system.

Govender’s writing has appeared in InSight+, the news and opinion publication of the Medical Journal of Australia, including essays on the advantages of working regionally and the healing power of art for doctors and their patients. Peer-reviewed work spans rheumatology and critical care, including coauthored research on vascular compression syndromes in Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and hypermobility spectrum disorder, a report in the International Journal of Rheumatic Diseases, and first-author research on surfactant and lung function after cardiac surgery. Govender shares updates on LinkedIn.

title: 7.7亿授权终止，这家浙江药企的转型棋局再生变数
summary: 2026年9月6日，浙江昂利康制药公告称，收到亚飞生物及亲合力通知，终止双方于2025年8月签署的关于IMD-1005药物分子的授权许可合作。该潜在交易总对价最高约7.7亿元，但因协议生效条件未满足，自始未发生法律效力，昂利康未支付任何款项，双方互不担责。此次终止并非项目失败，而是合作方基于自身能力评估，决定自主推进IMD-1005后续研发与商业化，暂不进行License-out。IMD-1005...
full_content:
9月6日晚，浙江昂利康制药股份有限公司（以下简称“昂利康”）发布公告称，公司近日收到亚飞（上海）生物医药科技有限公司（以下简称“亚飞生物”）及上海亲合力生物医药科技股份有限公司（以下简称“亲合力”）发来的《关于终止〈战略合作协议之授权许可协议〉的通知函》，双方此前围绕IMD-1005药物分子达成的授权许可合作终止推进。

 

 

时间回到一年前。

 

2025年8月26日，昂利康与亚飞生物、亲合力签署《战略合作协议之授权许可协议》，引进IMD-1005。亲合力拥有该药物分子的所有权，昂利康则获得该项目在中国大陆、中国香港、中国澳门及中国台湾地区的研发、生产和商业化独家权益，并将其内部命名为ALK-N002。根据协议，潜在交易总对价最高约7.7亿元，另附销售分成。

 

不过，7.7亿元并不意味着昂利康已经实际支付了这笔资金。原协议约定，授权许可协议需经亚飞生物董事会批准后方可生效。截至此次终止公告披露日，该生效条件仍未满足。根据公告，协议自始未发生法律效力，昂利康也未向合作方支付任何款项，双方互不承担违约责任。

 

与其说这是“一笔7.7亿元交易落空”，不如将其理解为：一项潜在总对价最高7.7亿元的License-in合作，在签署一年后，于正式履约前即宣告终止。



公告信息显示，IMD-1005项目本身并未终止，变化的是其商业化路径——合作方基于自身能力评估，决定自主推进后续研发与商业化，暂不通过License-out与第三方合作。

 

这一决策的背景，需要从IMD-1005的技术定位和合作方近期的能力变化两个维度来理解。

 

先看项目本身。IMD-1005是一款靶向CD47的肿瘤微环境激活型遮罩抗体。CD47是肿瘤免疫领域的重要靶点，通过与巨噬细胞表面的SIRPα结合，向免疫系统传递“别吃我”信号，因此阻断这一通路有望增强巨噬细胞对肿瘤细胞的吞噬。

 

这一机制曾吸引跨国药企重金押注。吉利德科学曾以约49亿美元收购Forty Seven，将magrolimab纳入管线；辉瑞则以约22.2亿美元收购Trillium Therapeutics，获得靶向CD47-SIRPα通路的候选药物。但由于CD47同时存在于正常血细胞表面，血液学毒性成为临床开发的重要挑战。近年来，magrolimab等项目陆续终止或调整，目前全球仍无CD47靶向药物获批上市。

 

IMD-1005的差异化之处，正在于其“遮罩”设计。根据昂利康此前披露，该药物在血液循环中暂时降低CD47抗体活性，进入肿瘤微环境后再解除遮罩、恢复靶向作用，试图在安全性与疗效之间取得更好的平衡。

 

再看合作方的变化。

 

过去两年，亚飞生物完成B2、B3轮融资，合计超过7亿元；与此同时，亲合力核心管线持续推进，平台技术也在不断拓展。随着资金储备和自主研发能力增强，资产持有方自然会重新计算“授权出去”与“自己推进”的收益与风险。

 

尤其对于IMD-1005这样的早期创新资产，如果后续临床能够验证其差异化设计的价值，自主推进意味着保留更多未来权益；反之，License-out则可以通过首付款、里程碑和合作方资源降低自身投入和开发风险。

 

因此，这次合作终止更适合被理解为一次License-out策略的重新调整，而非项目“失宠”或研发终止。至于合作方具体基于哪些内部判断作出这一决定，目前公告尚未进一步披露，仍有待后续进展验证。



对昂利康而言，IMD-1005并不是一笔孤立的License-in交易，而是其寻找第二增长曲线的一部分。

 

2024年2月，昂利康首次与亲合力合作，引进QHL-1618，并将其内部命名为ALK-N001；2025年8月，双方再次合作，就IMD-1005（ALK-N002）签署授权协议。连续两次引进肿瘤创新药，也意味着昂利康正尝试从传统化学制药业务向“仿创协同”模式延伸。

 

成立于2001年的昂利康，2018年登陆深交所，主营业务长期集中于化学原料药、制剂及特色中间体。

 

近年来，其传统业务增长承压。2026年上半年，公司实现营业收入6.27亿元，同比下降13.44%；归母净利润5492.64万元，同比下降16.68%。其中，制剂收入同比增长3.05%，但原料药和特色中间体收入分别下降13.85%和52.83%，成为整体业绩下滑的重要因素。

 

 

在这一背景下，创新药对于昂利康的意义并不只是增加几条管线，而是承载着业务结构调整的期待。

 

然而，随着ALK-N002合作终止，昂利康目前在研创新药布局重新集中于ALK-N001。后者目前仍处于临床早期阶段，这意味着公司原本计划通过连续引进外部创新资产来丰富管线的路径，出现了一定变化。

 

值得注意的是，昂利康此前还在推进创新药相关定增。公司曾计划募资约11.1亿元，其中包括创新药研发项目；ALK-N002也曾被纳入相关募集资金投资项目的调整计划。如今合作终止后，后续募资安排以及创新药资产引进策略是否调整，也成为市场关注的下一步。

 

对于昂利康而言，传统业务承压之下，如何建立真正能够支撑第二增长曲线的创新药资产，仍是一道需要继续回答的问题。



如果只看财务账面，此次终止对昂利康直接影响有限——无资金损失，无违约责任。但从战略层面看，它确实使公司通过License-in扩充管线的路径出现了一次调整。

 

更值得关注的是，这次终止并非昂利康主动放弃项目，而是合作方重新选择了商业化路径：不再通过License-out与第三方合作，而是将IMD-1005留在自身体系内推进。一进一退之间，恰好折射出传统药企通过License-in布局创新药时所面对的现实——拿到管线只是开始，真正决定转型成色的，是后续如何选择和投入。

 

过去几年，License-in成为不少传统药企切入创新药的重要方式。相比从零开始研发，引进外部资产能够更快获得创新药管线。但当项目进入临床开发阶段，企业最终仍要面对一个更现实的问题：拿到一项管线之后，是否值得继续投入？

 

一项创新药从临床走向商业化，需要持续投入资金、临床资源和研发能力。尤其对于传统业务承压、创新转型仍处于早期阶段的药企而言，管线数量本身并不等于转型速度。有限资源下，能否识别真正适合自身、具有临床价值和商业潜力的资产，并持续投入将其推进下去，反而更加重要。

 

因此，ALK-N002此次合作的终止，带来的启示并不只是昂利康少了一条创新药管线，而是让“拿管线”之后的问题更加具体：：License-in可以是传统药企转型创新药的入口，但管线选择和后续开发能力，才决定这条路能走多远。

 

对于昂利康如此，对于其他试图借助外部资产完成创新药转型的传统药企，同样如此。

title: 大模型驱动电子病历反向结构化：兼顾临床书写自由与数据治理
full_content:
来源：HIT专家网    作者：某特色医学中心信息科高级工程师孙建平

近日，笔者与医院肿瘤科主任围绕电子病历临床使用现状、人工智能在病历场景的落地方向开展交流。结合本次交流启发、院内AI探索实践，以及本院电子病历系统实际使用情况，笔者形成如下思考：借助大模型与自然语言处理技术，优化本院电子病历应用水平，推进病历质控与数据标准化升级，为电子病历智能化改造提供新方向。

结构化电子病历模板的临床使用情况分析

当前，笔者所在医院结构化电子病历模板的整体使用率不高。医护人员大多未完整使用系统预设的结构化录入格式，仅填报部分必填字段，其余诊疗内容主要通过手动自由编辑完成，结构化模板未能得到充分运用，主要原因有三点：

一是结构化录入流程较为繁琐。系统固定的逐项点选、分段填报模式，与临床高强度、快节奏的诊疗工作适配度不高，一定程度上增加了病历文书书写量。

二是通用模板专科适配性不足。通用病历模板的普适性较强，但针对专科病种、个体化病情的适配空间有限，难以充分满足复杂专科的精细化诊疗记录需求。

三是病历权限管控模式相对固定。系统对病历内容复制操作管控严格，与临床高效书写习惯存在适配冲突，一定程度影响病历录入效率。

笔者认为，临床未按模板书写形成的大量非结构化病历文本，恰恰为院内大模型应用创造了条件。这些存量病历的记录内容翔实，完整留存真实诊疗过程与临床思维，贴合本院实际，能够弥补传统结构化模板形式固化的不足，可用于探索训练贴合本院诊疗特点的专属医疗大模型。

在非结构化数据治理方面，可通过自然语言处理技术，自动完成病历自由文本的字段提取、语义归一、标准对齐。这一路径无需改造现有系统架构，也无需改变临床书写习惯，即可实现病历数据标准化治理，支持院内智能质控、临床数据分析、科研数据提取等工作。

反向结构化的具体思路

笔者设想依托大模型开展电子病历的反向结构化建设，具体思路如下：

1. 推行轻量、柔性结构化。针对医保上报、医疗质控、数据统计等刚需核心字段，严格落实国家标准化录入要求；放开病程分析、病情研判等个性化诊疗内容的编辑权限，通过柔性录入模式，兼顾合规要求与临床书写效率。

2. 搭建专科模块化动态模板。优化全院统一的模板体系，按科室、病种搭建可增删、可组合、可微调的模块化动态模板，适配肿瘤科等复杂专科的诊疗场景与个体化病情记录需求，弥补通用模板专科适配性不足的问题。

3. 优化病历内容复用机制。迭代现有固定的权限管控规则，建立溯源留痕、智能校验、风险预警的病历内容复用体系，在有效规避病历信息错配风险的前提下，适配临床高效书写习惯，提升病历录入效率。

4. 探索搭建院内专属AI全自动结构化模式。依托本院真实临床病历语料，探索训练适配院内诊疗场景的医疗大模型，通过自然语言解析技术，自动完成非结构化的病历文本的字段提取、语义归一、标准校正，借助AI技术完善院内病历数据治理体系。

反向结构化的核心逻辑是“临床柔性自由录入+AI后台自动标准化映射”，无需医生手动适配结构化字段，实现“书写自由、数据合规”。

一个具体的输入输出示例如下：

固定标准化录入部分（刚需字段，需要人工规范录入）：严格遵循国家病历规范，医保、质控、统计类核心字段统一标准化录入，如主诉、入院时间、诊断编码、手术方式、医保类型等必填字段，保证基础数据合规统一，满足质控与上报要求。

柔性自由录入部分（借助AI进行反向结构化处理）：医生针对病程记录、病情研判、诊疗思路等个性化内容，按照临床真实诊疗逻辑自由书写，无需拘泥于模板格式。

输入示例（非全结构化的医生原始书写内容）：“患者今日咳嗽、咳痰症状较前缓解，无胸闷、气喘不适，体温36.7℃，双肺听诊呼吸音粗，未闻及明显干湿性啰音，继续予抗感染、止咳化痰对症治疗，密切观察病情变化。”

AI反向结构化输出示例（自动归一、字段映射、标准化整理）：

【症状改善情况】咳嗽、咳痰症状较前好转；

【伴随症状】无胸闷、气喘；

【生命体征】体温36.7℃；

【体格检查】双肺呼吸音粗，无干湿性啰音；

【当前诊疗方案】维持抗感染、止咳化痰对症治疗；

【病情评估】病情平稳，持续监测病情。

通过该模式，既保留了临床病历的真实性、完整性、个性化，又在后台自动完成非全结构化文本的结构化拆解与语义标准化，解决了传统强制结构化“合规但不贴合临床”、自由文本“贴合临床但无法数据利用”的痛点。

工作思路与后续探索方向

本院电子病历系统已运行多年，在系统架构、数据标准方面与国家对电子病历规范化、智能化的建设要求存在一定差距，传统改造手段的提升空间有限。基于大模型开展反向结构化与智能质控等相关探索，无需大规模改造原有系统，既能对接国家合规标准，又贴合临床实际，具备较高的探索价值。

后续，我们将对标国家最新电子病历建设标准，立足本院系统现状，探索盘活院内存量非结构化的病历文本数据，以AI柔性标准化方案替代传统强制结构化模式，逐步完善院内病历标准化与质控规范化体系，为本院智慧医疗建设、临床数据深度挖掘应用提供研究支撑。

以上是笔者的一些思考，不当之处请大家批评指正。

title: Funding grants for new research into AI and teen development
summary: Apply now for OpenAI’s $5 million grant program supporting independent research on how generative AI affects teen development, well-being, and safety....
full_content:
OpenAI is committing $5 million to support independent research on how generative AI affects the lives and development of young people ages 13–17.

Generative AI is becoming part of how teens learn, create, and seek advice. Its effects are likely to be nuanced. They may depend on what teens use AI for, how they engage with it, their individual circumstances, and the support available from families, schools, communities, and technology providers.

We want to build a stronger evidence base about the way teens use AI, as well as the impacts of AI on their lives, to inform development of AI products for teens and to help answer major questions facing policymakers and regulators. For example, we aim to deepen industry-wide understanding of the nuances across age and context, efficacy of safeguards and interventions, and the ways that evidence can inform implementation and evaluation. This program will fund independent research into the opportunities and challenges associated with AI use during adolescence, with a particular focus on teens’ social and emotional development.

We welcome proposals that can deepen understanding and generate evidence relevant to current and emerging discourse, including:

  • How teens use generative AI and how different patterns of use relate to developmental outcomes
  • Potential impacts of AI use in teens’ lives
  • The individual, social, cultural, and technical factors that shape the effects of AI in teens’ lives
  • Technical interventions, safeguards, and design choices that can increase benefits or keep teens safer
  • How effects may differ across ages, developmental stages, populations, cultures, languages, and socioeconomic contexts

We welcome interdisciplinary research involving fields such as child and adolescent development, psychology, public health, human-computer interaction, communication, sociology, anthropology, data science, and AI safety. We encourage proposals from any country, and will prioritize those from countries with significant AI adoption.

Qualitative, quantitative, experimental, observational, theoretical, participatory, and mixed-methods approaches are all eligible. Research involving teens in the design or interpretation of studies is welcome but not required.

We encourage submissions that relate to one or more of the following topics:

  • Emotional development and well-being: Research on emotion regulation, resilience, identity, agency, self-esteem, and social connection.
  • Social development and relationships: Research on friendships, family relationships, belonging, communication, empathy, social skills, and the relationship between AI and human connection.
  • Patterns, contexts, and variance across demographics: Research on how outcomes vary by time spent, type and purpose of use, age, culture, language, socioeconomic circumstances, and other individual or contextual factors.
  • Mitigations, age-appropriate design, and policy approaches: Research evaluating safeguards, product interventions, AI literacy, parental or educator support, and healthy-use practices.

Research involving minors

Research involving minors requires particular attention to informed consent and assent, privacy, safeguarding, data security, and the possibility that participation may expose or generate sensitive information.

Applicants proposing research involving minors must explain:

  • The relevant institutional or independent ethics-review process
  • How informed consent and age-appropriate assent will be handled
  • How participants’ privacy and data will be protected
  • How researchers will respond to disclosures of harm or imminent risk
  • Whether the project involves sensitive personal, behavioral, or mental-health information
  • What relevant child-development, clinical, or safeguarding expertise the research team possesses
  • Parental consent, where appropriate

Collecting sensitive information does not automatically make a project ineligible. However, such projects may require additional ethical review, expertise, safeguards, and time.

Applications should be formatted as a single-spaced Google doc. Applicants should submit:

  • Project summary: A brief overview of the proposed research and its expected contribution, less than one page.
  • Research proposal: No more than three pages, excluding references, addressing:
    • Research questions
    • Relevant prior research
    • Proposed methods and analysis
    • Study population and recruitment strategy, including evidence of feasibility or access
    • Expected outputs
    • Potential limitations
    • Relevance to the program’s goals
  • Project plan and timeline: Key activities, milestones, and expected completion date.
  • Budget and budget justification: Requested funding, major cost categories, and any other committed sources of support.
  • Project dependencies: An explanation of requirements that must be met for the research to be carried out and risks that might endanger the project’s fruition.
  • Ethics and safeguarding statement: Required for any research involving minors, sensitive information, or potentially vulnerable populations. Where relevant, proposals should explicitly reference any regulation governing research with teens and compliance strategy.
  • Team information: Short CVs or bios for the principal investigator and key team members.
  • Independence and conflicts disclosure: Relevant financial relationships, industry funding, or other potential conflicts of interest.

Applications must be submitted in English. Research itself may be conducted in any language.

Proposals will be evaluated based on:

  • Scientific rigor: The strength and appropriateness of the research design and analysis
  • Relevance: Examination of a topic relevant to current public discourse on AI
  • Proposal quality: The clarity, focus, and coherence of the application
  • Actionability: The potential to translate findings into guidance for models, products, safeguards, regulatory approaches, or future research
  • Ethics and safeguarding: The adequacy of protections for minors and other participants
  • Feasibility: Whether the project can be completed with the proposed resources and timeline
  • Team expertise: The team’s ability to conduct the proposed work responsibly
  • Inclusion and generalizability: Attention to diverse populations, contexts, cultures, and experiences
  • Complementarity: The extent to which the work adds to existing evidence and complements OpenAI’s internal research agenda
  • Independence and credibility: The project’s ability to produce trustworthy findings regardless of whether those findings are favorable to providers of AI products

Preference may be given to research involving ChatGPT, interdisciplinary teams, underrepresented populations or regions, and projects capable of producing clear evidence that can inform near- or medium-term policy and regulatory decisions.

Final grants may be subject to the grantee’s execution of a grant agreement, award letter, certification, acknowledgment, or other documentation setting forth applicable terms and conditions. Grantees must accept and comply with any such requirements as a condition of receiving grant funding.

Submissions are open today through October 6, 2026. A panel of internal experts and advisors will review applications on a rolling basis and notify selected proposals on or before November 13, 2026. Follow this link⁠(opens in a new window) to apply⁠.

Q: What are the expected outputs?

A: Every funded project will be expected to provide OpenAI with a final report describing:

  • The research question and methods
  • Results and supporting evidence
  • Limitations and sources of uncertainty
  • Recommendations for policymakers, regulators, technology providers, or other stakeholders, where supported by the findings

To ensure research is progressing, we require an interim update on research progress and, where appropriate, an indication of early research findings in Q1 2027.

We are prioritizing research that can advance public dialogue on these critical topics. We strongly encourage researchers to make their findings publicly available through a peer-reviewed publication, preprint, public report, or similar format. However, publication will not be a condition of receiving funding.

Q: What are the eligibility criteria?

A: To be eligible, applicants must be:

  • 18 or older
  • Affiliated with a research institution or organization, and/or significant experience relevant to child or adolescent development, well-being, human-computer interaction, AI impacts, or a closely related field

Note that we are seeking to fund research rather than for-profit initiatives, so we will not prioritize for-profit organizations at this time.

Q: What budget is available per project?

A: We will award individual research grants up to $1 million and totaling up to $5 million.

Q: Can grant funds be used to cover overhead or indirect costs?

A: A maximum of 10% of each project’s grant can support overhead or indirect costs.

Q: Can grant funds be used to support student, graduate student, or post-doc involvement in research?

Q: Are these grants funded by OpenAI Foundation or OpenAI Group PBC?

A: The grants are funded and administered by OpenAI Group PBC.

Q: Who can I contact for questions about this grant?

A: Email collaborativeresearch@openai.com⁠. Note that we will not be providing status updates for individual applications that are not selected.

title: 【首发】威图医疗完成数千万元Pre-A轮融资，加码AI影像与全球化布局
summary: 2026年9月8日，宠物医疗CT影像设备及AI诊断企业威图医疗宣布完成数千万元人民币Pre-A轮融资，本轮融资由邦勤创投投资。威图医疗是全球宠物多功能CT影像设备的开创者及领航者，本轮融资资金将用于AI影像诊断研发、新一代影像成像技术迭代，以及海外营销与全球市场拓展。\n\n...
full_content:
近日，宠物医疗CT影像设备及AI诊断企业威图医疗宣布完成数千万元人民币Pre-A轮融资，本轮融资由邦勤创投投资。威图医疗是全球宠物多功能CT影像设备的开创者及领航者，本轮融资资金将用于AI影像诊断研发、新一代影像成像技术迭代，以及海外营销与全球市场拓展。


作为全球宠物多功能CT影像设备的开创者，威图医疗的产品与服务已覆盖全球23个国家和地区，累计服务超4500+家动物医院及科研机构。本轮融资的落地，是资本市场对公司在技术创新能力与商业化经营能力的认可与支持。




威图医疗成立于2017年，是一家专注于动物X射线（DR、CT）影像技术研发、生产与销售的国家级高新技术企业及专精特新企业，核心团队来自北京大学、清华大学、哈尔滨工业大学等国内顶尖高校。九年来，公司构建起覆盖硬件设计、软件开发与临床应用研究的高端医疗设备一体化研发体系，累计拥有42项自主知识产权，其中发明专利7项，技术触角延伸至CBCT伪影矫正、动态DR成像、X射线图像增强、动物磁共振成像(MRI)、PET-CT成像及多模态AI诊断等关键领域。



在产品端，威图医疗先后推出全球首台开放式宠物专用CBCT与国内首台宠物动态DR，形成以"CT+DR+AI智能设备"为核心的产品矩阵，全面覆盖从基层诊所到专科医院的多样化、智能化影像诊断需求。其中，新一代宠物多功能CT采用开放式架构与模块化设计，可在CT、DR、动态DR、C臂及DSA多种成像模式间无缝切换，以临床应用与优质图像质量重塑行业标准。



依托技术与产品的长期积累，威图医疗的全球化布局成效显著。公司业务现已覆盖中国、欧洲、东南亚等23个国家和地区，服务全球众多知名兽医医院和诊所；公司严格执行国际质量管理体系，已通过ISO13485质量管理体系认证及CE认证。依托持续的本地化服务与产品迭代，威图医疗正逐步形成“中国研发、全球销售”的竞争优势。



本轮投资方邦勤创投深耕医疗健康产业中早期投资，注重参与被投企业战略落地与经营发展。邦勤创投方面表示，威图医疗在兽用影像领域具备“硬件+软件+AI”全自研能力，在产品创新、成本控制、全球化市场拓展等方面展现出突出竞争力，精准契合宠物医疗行业对高性价比、智能化AI影像设备的刚性需求，有望成长为全球宠物CT设备领域的引领者。


 威图医疗创始人兼CEO杨飞表示：“首先感谢邦勤创投对威图医疗的认可与支持，本轮融资是资本市场对公司团队、技术和商业化成果的认可。全球宠物医疗正在经历从经验诊断到影像诊断、再到智能诊断的升级过程，威图在宠物诊疗升级需求推动下有望成长为全球动物影像服务的“IDEXX爱德士”。本轮融资也让我们有能力和实力在AI影像技术上走得更深更远，也有机会把中国供应链优势转化为全球市场的产品竞争力。


面向未来，威图医疗将继续坚持以自主研发为根本，推动AI技术与影像硬件设备深度融合，打造动物CT设备及AI诊断的引领者品牌，让更多凝聚中国智造的宠物医疗创新产品走向全球，服务全球兽医与动物医疗健康事业。


 


威图医疗成立于2017年，是一家专注于宠物智能医疗设备及AI诊断服务的国家级高新技术企业，业务聚焦动物X射线（DR、CT）影像技术的研发、生产与销售，是业内少数具备“硬件研发+影像软件自研+AI建模诊断”完整技术能力的厂商之一。公司总部位于深圳，核心团队来自北京大学、清华大学、哈尔滨工业大学等高校；已获得42项自主知识产权授权，其中发明专利7项；已通过ISO13485质量管理体系认证及CE认证，累计服务超4500+家宠物医院及科研机构，业务覆盖全球23个国家和地区。



邦勤创投是一家总部位于深圳的私募基金管理人，专注投资于医疗健康、人工智能等领域，围绕“生、死、美、爽”四大方向，以“强刚需、硬科技”为原则选择标的，在管规模十数亿元，已投资项目近50个，凭借不俗的投资业绩，荣获深圳天使母基金优秀子基金，投中榜、融中邦top10等荣誉。

title: 双院士团队领衔，多家顶尖医院完成心流®首植！见证国产pVAD商业化启航
summary: 8月中旬，由葛均波院士领衔的“pVAD疗法中国临床应用启幕大会”圆满落幕，标志着国产介入式左心室辅助装置SynFlow®\u002F心流® 3.0正式开启商业化进程。会后，葛均波院士团队在复旦大学附属中山医院成功完成首例高危PCI手术，利用该设备为LVEF仅30%的复杂患者提供循环支持，并获环太平洋地区专家访问团现场观摩与高度评价。丰凯利医疗通过创新的电机分离技术，将一次性耗材中最昂贵的电机移至体...
full_content:
8月中旬，由北京华夏公益基金会主办的“pVAD疗法中国临床应用启幕大会暨全国pVAD临床专家首次线上MDT讨论会”圆满落幕。本场专题会特邀复旦大学附属中山医院葛均波院士担任会议主席，来自全球多家中心的心血管专家围绕pVAD的临床应用展开了深入讨论。


随着国产pVAD逐步进入临床应用阶段，如何建立更符合中国患者特征与临床实际的真实世界证据体系，并进一步推动治疗支付与临床可及性，成为行业下一阶段需要面对的重要课题。


理念的讨论很快延伸到了手术台。会后，葛均波院士团队在复旦大学附属中山医院心内科导管室完成了一台高危PCI手术：患者心脏泵血能力（LVEF）仅30%，合并复杂多支冠脉病变，其中前降支完全闭塞。面对这一高风险手术，团队选择使用国产介入式左心室辅助装置SynFlow®/心流® 3.0提供循环支持，在维持血流动力学稳定的基础上，顺利完成后续介入治疗。


 葛均波院士接待环太平洋地区的心血管专家访问团


当天，中山医院还迎来了一支来自环太平洋地区的心血管专家访问团。海外专家专程现场观摩了这台手术，也注意到了术中使用的这款国产pVAD。术后，交流很快从手术本身延伸到产品层面，他们很好奇这款设备叫什么？性能如何？价格贵不贵？


复旦大学附属中山医院副院长钱菊英教授向到访专家介绍：这是SynFlow®/心流® 3.0，由中国企业丰凯利医疗自主研发，价格仅为国外同类产品的三分之一。


 钱菊英教授向环太平洋国家心内专家访问团介绍SynFlow®/心流® 3.0


这场交流也映照出pVAD临床应用背后的共同需求：无论中国还是海外，医生都希望在满足临床性能需求的基础上，为患者提供更加可及的治疗方案。就pVAD而言，其性能决定了临床“能不能用”，价格则进一步决定了“能不能让更多患者用到”。


而“高质量普惠”，恰恰是SynFlow®/心流® 3.0项目立项的初心。丰凯利从创立之初便另辟蹊径选择了电机分离技术路线——将一次性耗材中最昂贵的电机移至体外、重复使用，在满足循环辅助需求的同时改变产品的成本结构，让单次使用成本大幅下降。


但产品设计理念最终能否成立，还需要接受真实临床应用的检验。


就在这场大会召开后，丰凯利“心流®大师体验周”在全国展开：两周时间，SynFlow®/心流® 3.0先后进入多家头部心血管中心，完成十余例手术且全部成功。一款上市仅两个月的国产pVAD，就此完成了上市后第一轮集中的真实世界验证——这样的临床推进速度，并不常见。



“快”只是表象，真正值得关注的是：SynFlow®/心流® 3.0为何能在短时间内进入多家头部医院？它又凭什么能在不同中心、不同病例和不同术者手中，完成稳定可靠的连续应用？



先看这份首植名单的含金量（按首字母排序）：复旦大学附属中山医院、广东省人民医院南海医院、南方医科大学南方医院、首都医科大学附属北京安贞医院、武汉亚洲心脏病医院、西安交通大学第一附属医院、浙江大学医学院附属第二医院、中国人民解放军总医院。8家中心全部位于国内心血管领域的第一梯队，地域上覆盖华北、华东、华南、华中、西北。


更值得注意的是使用节奏（按首字母排序）：广东省人民医院南海医院、南方医科大学南方医院、首都医科大学附属北京安贞医院、西安交通大学第一附属医院、浙江大学医学院附属第二医院在完成首例后，紧接着开展了第二例——“首植即连用”，本身就是临床认可最直接的证据。


值得关注的是，此次首批植入的病例中，也不乏对器械极具考验的极限场景。


中国人民解放军总医院陈韵岱教授团队的田峰教授和周珊珊教授，面对的是一位老年女性患者，该高龄患者合并糖尿病、肾功能不全、中度贫血及电解质紊乱等多系统疾病，心梗入院，心功能弥漫性下降（EF仅28%），入院时已出现频发室颤，冠脉造影显示三支血管病变，罪犯病变为LAD开口重度狭窄、支架内再狭窄，重度钙化。


团队采用SynFlow®/心流® 3.0pVAD预防性置入策略，在操作启动前即建立稳定血流动力学平台，成功实现了循环保障关口前移，在IVL震波预处理、球囊扩张及多支架植入等操作期间，患者未出现低血压、恶性心律失常或循环崩溃。


术后，周珊珊教授从实际操作体验出发，提到：“SynFlow®/心流® 3.0在送入和撤出过程中整体非常顺畅，这体现出产品设计对临床细节的重视：例如穿导丝时配有引导性小管结构，可协助导丝平顺进入主管腔，降低其从侧孔异常穿出的风险，这些细节都提升了操作手感与临床舒适度。”



pVAD并非普通的高值介入耗材，此前也未在国内广泛普及。从患者筛选、术前评估，到器械准备、术者培训，再到手术当天的跟台支持，链条长、环节多，任何一个环节出现衔接不畅，都可能影响产品进入临床应用的效率。


因此，高密度、多中心的首植落地，考验的不只是产品质量的一致性与稳定性，更是企业从生产供应、备货交付到临床支持的全链条保障能力。例如此次半个月，8家头部中心、十余位医生同步完成患者筛选与手术排期，且每例手术均有专业人员跟台保障，其核心难点在于“多线并行”。



落到具体执行层面，丰凯利团队及合作伙伴在医院端要同步协调不同中心的准入、试用及手术安排，临床端则要围绕患者筛选、术前沟通和术中操作全程护航——任何一条线掉链子，都会打乱整体节奏。这种多中心同步走通、互不干扰的推进能力，充分彰显了丰凯利团队强大的统筹协同实力。


而支撑这套高密度推进节奏的，是一支“边组建、边打仗”的商业化团队。丰凯利通过吸纳成熟的市场、销售与临床人才，实现业务的快速推进与拓展。这次密集首植本身，就是对这支新锐部队实战能力的一次全面检验。



高效的执行团队或许能把产品送进医院，而能否形成常态化的临床应用，最终取决于产品本身。


SynFlow®/心流® 3.0是全球唯一获批的电机分离技术路线pVAD。通过攻克长距离柔性传动、旋转与密封，以及机械摩擦、润滑与磨损微粒管理等技术难题，丰凯利将原本集成于一次性高值耗材中的电机部分移至体外，并转化为可重复使用的设备；辅以丰凯利独创的Clinfusion®洁净灌注技术，在有效维持血流动力学稳定的同时，既避免了电机体内高温升带来的溶血、血栓等风险，也避免了磨损微粒对患者的二次伤害，在保证性能的同时显著降低了产品成本，更契合中国当前的支付体系。


循证层面，就在不久前的7月29日，复旦大学附属中山医院葛均波、钱菊英以及中国人民解放军总医院陈韵岱等发表在《欧洲心脏杂志》的PERSIST Ⅲ研究表明，在高危PCI手术期间预防性使用我国自主研发的微轴流泵SynFlow®/心流® 3.0，在30天主要不良事件发生率方面不劣于静脉-动脉体外膜氧合（VA-ECMO），且使用微轴流泵的患者术后住院时间更短，设备相关不良事件更少，贫血发生率也更低。



而在循证数据之外，来自本次试用各中心一线术者的反馈，构成了SynFlow®/心流® 3.0在真实世界的第一份“用户报告”。其中，多位医生提到，SynFlow®/心流® 3.0并没有要求介入医生重新建立一套陌生的操作体系，其操作方法与主动脉内球囊反搏（IABP）类似，只是多了跨瓣和放泵两步，医生可以快速上手。


广东省人民医院南海医院罗建方教授表示，SynFlow®/心流® 3.0作为左心室引流泵，可将左心室血流引流至主动脉，同时减轻心脏前负荷与后负荷，较IABP具有明显优势。从完成的首例应用来看，其效果良好，且血流动力学不依赖心率变化，整个过程相当平稳。从设计上看，该产品将电机置于体外，可减少因升温导致的溶血等血液成分损伤；同时作为国产设备，其操作便捷、使用安全——在PCI过程中，即使因导管阻断血流引起血压波动，患者心电及血流动力学仍保持平稳，这与使用IABP时的体验有所不同。总体而言，该装置的应用前景广阔，不仅适用于高危PCI，也可用于已有心功能不全甚至休克状态的患者，以及结构性心脏病（如二尖瓣）介入治疗后左室功能恢复不良的患者，能够有效帮助心脏减负。


浙江大学医学院附属第二医院王建安院士团队蒋峻教授认为，pVAD最大的优势在于流量支持显著强于IABP，且操作比ECMO简单。从前期的临床试验和试用经验来看，SynFlow®/心流® 3.0与国外同类产品相比，最大的改进在于电机外置设计：一方面可避免体内装置对电池的干扰；另一方面，电机外置后可以实现复用，从而显著降低导管成本。对pVAD而言，价格是目前临床推广最大的制约因素之一，因此能够有效控制成本的器械，将对临床普及和患者使用带来很大益处。


首都医科大学附属北京安贞医院祖晓麟教授评价道，IABP仅能提供约1 L/min的有限左室辅助，这种辅助在面对病变更复杂、操作时间更长的高危PCI时常显不足；SynFlow®/心流® 3.0作为主动轴可显著提升循环支持能力。其植入过程建立在左室造影基础之上，路径与介入医生成长训练相匹配，有经验的介入医生无需掌握特殊操作技巧和策略，即熟练完成。过去受技术壁垒限制，国内缺乏像Impella一样的左室辅助装置，许多高危操作只能相对冒险完成；如今国产左室轴流泵问世，为高危复杂PCI提供了极大的保障。对于急性心梗后迅速出现心功能不全、心衰甚至休克趋势的患者，根本仍是尽早完成血运重建；左室轴流泵的出现真正实现了对急性心梗合并左室功能不全患者立竿见影，甚至是力挽狂澜的治疗效果。


让更多患者用得起，丰凯利加速SynFlow®/心流®3.0走向临床


短期内的高密度首植初步验证了SynFlow®/心流® 3.0的临床落地能力，多中心连续应用以及一线术者的实际反馈，则进一步检验了产品的操作体验、性能表现与临床接受度。对丰凯利而言，下一步命题已然明晰：如何把已形成的临床势能，转化为更大范围的医院覆盖和持续应用，让更多患者用得起。


支撑这一命题的，是临床需求本身。在国内，每年都有大量高危PCI和心功能不全患者，因术中循环风险而无法获得充分的血运重建；对医生而言，他们需要的并不只是一个“国产替代”，而是一款性能可靠、操作顺手，同时能够让患者真正承担得起的pVAD。毕竟，pVAD发展的最终目的，是能让更多患者尽早获得合适的治疗选择。


这也构成了丰凯利持续推进产品创新与临床应用的出发点。


SynFlow®/心流® 3.0是全球唯一获批的电机分离型pVAD，电机可复用的设计有望显著降低使用成本，更契合中国支付体系。在此基础上，PERSIST系列研究提供了不劣于VA-ECMO的循证证据；多中心连续应用及“首植即连用”的临床反馈，则进一步验证了SynFlow®/心流® 3.0在真实世界中的稳定可靠。


而从获批后的快速响应，到“心流®大师体验周”期间多家头部中心的集中应用，丰凯利的快速推进，也是团队临床执行能力的直接呈现……这三方面能力，最终指向了同一个目标：即更好、更快地满足临床需求。


从这个角度看，丰凯利不仅用多中心密集首植的惊艳成绩单证明了自身实力，更证明了一件事：当国产pVAD能同时回答好“性能”与“可及性”两个问题时，临床的接受可以来得很快。


从首批中心走向更多医院，从首批试用走向常规应用，从“医生愿意用”到“形成稳定使用”，国产pVAD的下半场已经开场。而率先跑通“获批—进院—首植—连用”全程的丰凯利，正在把技术优势转化为真实的临床覆盖——


这场竞赛的终点线不在对手身上，而在一个个仍等待治疗机会的患者面前。首批临床应用只是起点，接下来，丰凯利会让SynFlow®/心流® 3.0抵达更多真正需要它的患者。
